n: Israel sins again, and the Philistines rule them for forty years — the longest oppression in Judges. Notice that this time Israel doesn’t even cry out for help.

f.g: A sea-people from the Aegean region who settled Canaan’s southern coast, skilled in iron-working.

n: In Zorah lives Manoah of Dan, whose wife cannot have children. Like Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and Hannah, she will bear a son by God’s gift.
The angel of the Lord appears to the woman and promises she will have a son. God’s message comes first to her, not her husband.

f.w: the angel of the LORD appeared unto the woman

n: Even during pregnancy she must avoid wine, strong drink, and unclean food, because her son will be set apart from conception.

f.g: Beer or other fermented drink.

n: The son will be a Nazarite from the womb — never cutting his hair — and will begin to rescue Israel from the Philistines. “Begin” is key: David would finish the job.

f.g: From Hebrew nazir, “consecrated” or “separated”; not related to Nazareth.

n: She tells her husband that a man of God came, awe-inspiring like an angel. She didn’t ask his name.

f.g: Awe-inspiring, fearsome.
A common title for a prophet or messenger.

n: She repeats the message, adding that the child will be a Nazarite “to the day of his death” — a hint of the story’s end.

f.w: to the day of his death

n: Manoah prays for the man to return and teach them how to raise the child. A good model: parents seeking God’s help to raise children.

f.w: teach us what we shall do unto the child

f.g: Prayed, pleaded with.

n: God answers Manoah’s prayer, but the angel again appears to his wife in the field while Manoah is away.

f.g: God listened and answered.

n: She runs to bring her husband.

f.g: Hurried.

n: Manoah follows her and asks if this is the man who spoke to her. He says, “I am.”

f.g: A simple “Yes”; compare the divine name in Exodus 3:14.

n: Manoah asks how they should raise the boy and what his life will be.

f.w: How shall we order the child
f.g: What rule should govern the child’s life?

n: The angel simply repeats: let her follow everything I already said.

f.g: Be careful to observe.

n: She must avoid all grape products, wine, strong drink, and unclean food — following the Nazarite rules herself during pregnancy.

f.w: any thing that cometh of the vine

n: Manoah offers the hospitality of a meal, still thinking the visitor is a man.

f.g: Young goat.

n: The angel declines food but says any burnt offering should go to the Lord. Manoah doesn’t yet understand who he is.
Manoah asks the visitor’s name so they can honor him when the promise comes true.
The angel answers that his name is “secret” — literally “wonderful,” beyond understanding. Isaiah uses the same root for the Messiah: “his name shall be called Wonderful.”

f.g: Hebrew pil’i, “wonderful, beyond comprehension.”

n: Manoah offers a young goat and grain on a rock to the Lord, and the angel does something wonderful while they watch.

f.g: Grain offering.
The same Hebrew root as the “wonderful” name in verse 18.

n: As the flame rises, the angel ascends in it to heaven. Manoah and his wife fall on their faces in awe.
The angel doesn’t appear again. Now Manoah realizes who he was.

f.g: Finally understood.

n: Manoah fears they will die because they have seen God.
His wife reasons wisely: if God wanted to kill us, He wouldn’t have accepted our offering or told us these promises. Her faith steadies his fear.

f.w: If the LORD were pleased to kill us
f.g: She draws comfort from what God has already done.

n: She names her son Samson, and the Lord blesses him as he grows.

f.g: Probably from Hebrew shemesh, “sun” — perhaps “little sun.”

n: The Spirit of the Lord begins to stir him in Dan’s camp between Zorah and Eshtaol. His gifts come from God from the start.

f.g: Stir or impel him, like a sudden push.
Hebrew Mahaneh-dan, also a place name.
